uno.name: Arduino Uno R3
notes: The Uno runs at 5 V: a HIGH output pin sits near 5 V and its inputs read HIGH above roughly 3 V.
Each I/O pin can safely source or sink about 40 mA — an LED without a resistor asks for far more and damages the pin.
analogRead() returns 0–1023 (10 bits) for 0–5 V, so one step is about 4.9 mV.
Only pins D3, D5, D6, D9, D10 and D11 (marked ~) support analogWrite() PWM at about 490 Hz.
A0–A5 double as digital pins 14–19; A4/A5 are also the I2C SDA/SCL lines used by LCD and sensor modules.
int is 16 bits here: values above 32,767 wrap around to negative numbers — use long for big counters.
The board is powered over USB; the 5V pin can supply about 500 mA in total to your circuit.
External interrupts are available on D2 and D3 (attachInterrupt).

nano.name: Arduino Nano
notes: The Nano is an Uno shrunk onto a breadboard-friendly stick: same 5 V logic, same 16 MHz chip, same pin numbers.
It straddles the breadboard gap — the two pin rows are 6 pitches apart, so the top row lands in column b and the bottom row in column f.
Pins A6 and A7 are analog-input only: analogRead works, digitalWrite does not.
Like the Uno, only D3, D5, D6, D9, D10 and D11 offer PWM with analogWrite().
analogRead() returns 0–1023 (10 bits) for 0–5 V.
Each pin is limited to about 40 mA; always put a resistor in series with an LED.
A4 is SDA and A5 is SCL for I2C modules such as the 16x2 LCD backpack.

esp32.name: ESP32 DevKit V1
notes: The ESP32 is a 3.3 V board. Its GPIO pins tolerate at most about 3.6 V — 5 V on a pin burns it. Use a voltage divider or a level shifter for 5 V sensors.
VIN carries the 5 V from USB and can power 5 V modules; 3V3 is the regulated 3.3 V that the chip itself runs on.
analogRead() returns 0–4095 (12 bits) for 0–3.3 V — remember to change 1023 to 4095 when porting Uno code.
ADC2 pins (GPIO 2, 4, 12–15, 25–27) stop working while WiFi is connected; use ADC1 pins (GPIO 32–39) for sensors in IoT projects.
GPIO 34, 35, 36 and 39 are input-only: they can read but never drive an LED.
Nine header pins are capacitive touch inputs (T0 = GPIO4 … T9 = GPIO32): touchRead() drops from about 70 to about 15 when a finger touches the pad.
Any output pin can do PWM through the LEDC peripheral (analogWrite or ledcWrite); GPIO25/26 are true 8-bit DACs.
int is 32 bits and the chip runs at 240 MHz — millions of statements per second, so short delays matter more than loop overhead.

esp32s3.name: ESP32-S3 DevKitC-1
notes: The ESP32-S3 is a 3.3 V board like the classic ESP32: never feed a GPIO more than 3.6 V.
The 5V pin passes the USB supply through for 5 V modules; the chip itself and its 3V3 pins run at 3.3 V.
GPIO1–GPIO20 are 12-bit ADC inputs (0–4095). GPIO1–10 are ADC1 (WiFi-safe); GPIO11–20 are ADC2 and pause while WiFi is up.
GPIO1–GPIO14 are touch pads T1–T14 — the S3 has more touch channels than any other board here.
There is no DAC on the S3: use PWM (ledcWrite) and an RC filter when you need an analog-like output.
The built-in RGB LED lives on GPIO48; the default I2C bus is SDA = GPIO8, SCL = GPIO9.
GPIO43/44 are the UART0 TX/RX lines used by the serial monitor; GPIO19/20 are the native USB data pins.
GPIO0, GPIO45 and GPIO46 are strapping pins read at boot — they still work as I/O but avoid pulling them the wrong way at power-up.

raspberrypi4.name: Raspberry Pi 4 Model B
notes: The 40-pin header uses 3.3 V GPIO. Physical header numbers and BCM GPIO numbers differ.
The simulator accepts a documented Python subset with gpiozero and RPi.GPIO-compatible calls.
There is no built-in analog input. ADCs, Linux, networking, cameras and external Python packages are not simulated.
GPIO resistance, current limits and virtual instruction timing are teaching-model approximations.

raspberrypi5.name: Raspberry Pi 5
notes: The 40-pin header uses 3.3 V GPIO. Physical header numbers and BCM GPIO numbers differ.
The simulator accepts a documented Python subset with gpiozero and RPi.GPIO-compatible calls.
There is no built-in analog input. ADCs, Linux, networking, cameras and external Python packages are not simulated.
GPIO resistance, current limits and virtual instruction timing are teaching-model approximations.

learn.summary: The Arduino Uno is the classic 5 V microcontroller board. Your sketch runs setup() once, then loop() forever, and each pin becomes an output (drives 0 V or 5 V) or an input (reads a voltage) depending on pinMode().
pinout: D0–D13: digital I/O. D13 also drives the built-in LED (LED_BUILTIN).
~D3, ~D5, ~D6, ~D9, ~D10, ~D11: PWM-capable — analogWrite(pin, 0..255).
A0–A5: analog inputs (0–5 V → 0–1023); usable as digital pins 14–19. A4 = SDA, A5 = SCL.
5V / 3V3 / VIN: supply pins. GND ×3: all the same ground.
D0 (RX) / D1 (TX): the USB serial link — avoid them for your circuits.
tips: Always connect a GND pin to the breadboard's − rail first; every circuit needs a return path.
Power the + rail from 5V for LEDs and modules; use 3V3 only for parts that say so.
A pin can only supply about 40 mA. Put a 220 Ω resistor in series with every LED.
Set pinMode(pin, INPUT_PULLUP) for buttons and wire the button to GND — no extra resistor needed.
formulas: LED current I = (5 V − Vf) / (R + 25 Ω)   (25 Ω is the pin's own output resistance)
pitfalls: int is 16-bit: 40 × 1000 overflows to −25536. Use long or unsigned long for millis() math.
Shorting 5V to GND trips the USB supply — nothing lights up and everything gets warm.

learn.summary: The Arduino Nano is the Uno's little sibling: the same chip, the same 5 V pins and sketches, on a board that plugs straight into the breadboard.
pinout: Top row (D13, 3V3, AREF, A0–A7, 5V, RST, GND, VIN) and bottom row (D12–D2, GND, RST, RX0, TX1) straddle the breadboard gap.
D13 drives the built-in LED; ~D3, ~D5, ~D6, ~D9, ~D10, ~D11 are PWM pins.
A0–A5 are analog + digital; A6 and A7 are analog-input only.
A4 = SDA and A5 = SCL for I2C displays and sensors.
tips: Place the Nano with its top row in column b — the bottom row then lands in column f, leaving a–a and g–j free for wires.
Each Nano pin gets its own 5-hole row strip, so wire parts to the strip rather than trying to reach the pin itself.
Use the two GND pins to feed both − rails so wiring stays short.
formulas: LED current I = (5 V − Vf) / (R + 25 Ω)
pitfalls: Rotating the Nano 90° never fits: the 15-pin rows are longer than the breadboard is tall.

learn.summary: The ESP32 DevKit V1 is a 3.3 V, 32-bit microcontroller with built-in WiFi. It is far faster than an Uno and adds touch sensing, a 12-bit ADC and two DACs — but its pins are NOT 5 V tolerant.
pinout: GPIOn pins: any of them can be a digital input/output and PWM output (ledcWrite / analogWrite).
GPIO34, 35, 36 (VP) and 39 (VN): input-only, ADC1 — the best pins for analog sensors when WiFi is on.
T0 = GPIO4, T2 = GPIO2, T3 = GPIO15, T4 = GPIO13, T5 = GPIO12, T6 = GPIO14, T7 = GPIO27, T8 = GPIO33, T9 = GPIO32: touch pads.
GPIO25 / GPIO26: 8-bit DAC outputs. GPIO21 = SDA, GPIO22 = SCL. GPIO2 = built-in LED.
VIN: 5 V from USB for 5 V modules. 3V3: the 3.3 V logic supply. GND ×2.
tips: Anchor the board at column a (row 1): the pins land in a and i, leaving row j free below. Dual-board mode exposes rows on both sides.
LEDs still need a resistor, but current is lower at 3.3 V: 220 Ω with a red LED gives about 6 mA.
For a 5 V sensor output (HC-SR04 echo), use a 1 kΩ / 2.2 kΩ divider or a level shifter before the GPIO.
Read pots and LDRs on ADC1 pins (GPIO32–39); ADC2 pins return 0 while WiFi is connected.
formulas: Divider output Vout = Vin × R2 / (R1 + R2)   →   5 V × 2.2 k / 3.2 k = 3.44 V
pitfalls: Feeding more than 3.6 V into a GPIO burns it — VIN, 5 V modules and Uno outputs are all dangerous.
Porting Uno code: 1023 becomes 4095, and delay() is the same but the loop runs about 15× faster.

learn.summary: The ESP32-S3 DevKitC-1 is the newer, wider ESP32: still 3.3 V and WiFi-capable, with 14 touch pads, 20 ADC pins, native USB and an on-board RGB LED. It bridges a dual breadboard with 22 pins per side.
pinout: GPIO1–GPIO20: 12-bit ADC inputs (ADC1 = GPIO1–10, ADC2 = GPIO11–20) and T1–T14 touch pads on GPIO1–14.
GPIO8 = SDA, GPIO9 = SCL (default Wire bus). GPIO48 = on-board RGB LED (LED_BUILTIN).
GPIO43 (TX) / GPIO44 (RX): UART0 — the serial monitor. GPIO19 / GPIO20: native USB D− / D+.
5V passes the USB supply through; both 3V3 pins are the 3.3 V logic supply. GND ×4.
tips: The S3 spans 22 rows — anchor it at row 1 and use dual-board mode so both pin rows are reachable.
Use ADC1 (GPIO1–10) for analog sensors in WiFi projects.
There is no DAC: create analog-ish output with PWM and an RC filter.
pitfalls: Never connect 5 V to a GPIO — same 3.6 V limit as every ESP32.
GPIO0, GPIO45 and GPIO46 decide the boot mode; a pull-down on GPIO0 at power-up keeps the board in the bootloader.

learn.summary: A Raspberry Pi single-board computer with a 40-pin GPIO header for Python electronics projects.
pinout: BCM17 is physical pin 11; BCM27 is physical pin 13.
3V3: physical pins 1 and 17. 5V: physical pins 2 and 4.
GND: physical pins 6, 9, 14, 20, 25, 30, 34 and 39.
tips: Use BCM pin numbers with gpiozero.
Use a series resistor for LEDs and a transistor driver for motors.
pitfalls: GPIO is not 5 V tolerant.
Analog sensors need an external ADC; it is not simulated yet.

learn.summary: A Raspberry Pi single-board computer with a 40-pin GPIO header for Python electronics projects.
pinout: BCM17 is physical pin 11; BCM27 is physical pin 13.
3V3: physical pins 1 and 17. 5V: physical pins 2 and 4.
GND: physical pins 6, 9, 14, 20, 25, 30, 34 and 39.
tips: Use BCM pin numbers with gpiozero.
Use a series resistor for LEDs and a transistor driver for motors.
pitfalls: GPIO is not 5 V tolerant.
Analog sensors need an external ADC; it is not simulated yet.

learn.summary: A resistor limits current. Push a voltage across it and a predictable current flows: the bigger the resistance, the smaller the current. Its value is printed as colour bands.
pinout: p1 / p2: no polarity — either way round works.
Spans 5 holes: bridge two different row strips (or the gap between the a–e and f–j blocks).
tips: 220 Ω is the go-to value for an LED on a 5 V pin (about 13 mA); 1 kΩ gives a dimmer, safer 3 mA.
10 kΩ is the standard pull-up / pull-down and the standard partner for an LDR or thermistor divider.
Read the bands from the side where they are closer together; the gold band is the tolerance (±5 %).
formulas: Ohm's law: V = I × R   →   I = V / R
LED current: I = (Vsrc − Vf) / (R + Rpin + rOn)
Power dissipated: P = V × I = I² × R  (a 1/4 W resistor is fine below 0.25 W)
pitfalls: Both legs in the same 5-hole strip short the resistor out — the current simply bypasses it.
Too small a value (or none at all) lets an LED draw far more than its 30 mA limit: smoke.

learn.summary: A capacitor stores charge. It smooths sudden voltage dips and filters noise. In this DC simulation it behaves like an open circuit once charged — no steady current flows through it.
pinout: pos (+): the longer leg / unmarked side of an electrolytic can.
neg (−): the shorter leg, marked with a stripe.
tips: Place 100 µF across a module's VCC and GND to keep servos and NeoPixels from resetting your board.
Values are in microfarads (µF); bigger stores more energy but charges slower.
formulas: RC time constant: τ = R × C  (63 % charged after one τ)
pitfalls: Electrolytic capacitors are polarised — connect + to the higher voltage or they vent in real life.
Because DC is simulated, you will not see blink timing change with the capacitor here.

learn.summary: A rectifier diode is a one-way valve for current: it conducts from anode to cathode once about 0.7 V is across it and blocks the other way. Use it to protect against reversed polarity or motor kick-back.
pinout: anode (+): current enters here.
cathode (−): the end with the silver stripe; current leaves here.
tips: Place it "backwards" across a motor or relay coil (cathode to +) as a flyback diode.
It drops about 0.7 V, so a 5 V supply through a diode gives roughly 4.3 V.
pitfalls: Reversed, it blocks completely — a "dead" circuit is often a backwards diode.
Rated for 1 A here; a direct short across a supply still exceeds that.

learn.summary: An NPN transistor is an electronic switch and amplifier. A small current into the base lets a current up to about 100 times larger flow from collector to emitter — so a 40 mA pin can control a 300 mA motor.
pinout: e (emitter): connect to GND.
b (base): drive from a pin through a 1–10 kΩ resistor.
c (collector): the load (motor, relay, LED strip) sits between + and here.
tips: Always add a base resistor: 1 kΩ from a 5 V pin gives about 4 mA of base current, enough for ~400 mA of load.
When fully on (saturated) the collector sits at about 0.2 V — nearly a closed switch.
Combine with a flyback diode across motors and relay coils.
formulas: Collector current (active): Ic = β × Ib, β ≈ 100
pitfalls: Base straight to a pin without a resistor pulls far more than 40 mA — the pin overheats.
Flat-face pinout of a 2N2222 is E-B-C left to right; swapping E and C makes it barely conduct.

learn.summary: An LED lights when current flows from anode to cathode, but only after its forward voltage (about 1.8 V red … 2.8 V white) is reached. It has almost no resistance of its own, so a series resistor sets the current.
pinout: anode (+): the longer leg — connect toward the positive side / MCU pin.
cathode (−): the shorter leg on the flat side of the lens — connect toward GND.
tips: Brightness follows current: ~13 mA (220 Ω on 5 V) is bright, ~3 mA (1 kΩ) is a soft glow.
On a 3.3 V board the same 220 Ω gives about 6 mA for red and just 2 mA for blue — still visible.
Reversed LEDs simply stay dark; they are not damaged at these voltages.
pitfalls: No resistor: (5 V − 1.8 V) / 10 Ω ≈ 320 mA — the LED pops and the pin is overloaded (40 mA max).
Both legs in the same breadboard strip short the LED — it never lights.

learn.summary: An RGB LED is three LEDs (red, green, blue) in one lens sharing a common cathode. Mix colours by driving the three anodes with PWM.
pinout: r: red anode (Vf ≈ 1.8 V).
cathode: the longest leg — to GND.
g: green anode (≈ 2.1 V).
b: blue anode (≈ 2.7 V).
tips: Each colour needs its own series resistor (220 Ω); one shared resistor makes the colours fight each other.
Use three PWM pins and analogWrite(r, 255) analogWrite(g, 128) analogWrite(b, 0) for orange.
formulas: Per channel: I = (Vsrc − Vf_channel) / (R + Rpin + rOn)
pitfalls: Blue needs the highest Vf, so it is dimmest at 3.3 V — increase its duty or lower its resistor.

learn.summary: A piezo buzzer clicks every time the voltage across it changes; drive it with tone(pin, frequency) and the clicks become a note. Electrically it looks like about 1 kΩ, so a pin drives it directly.
pinout: pos (+): to the tone pin.
neg (−): to GND.
tips: tone(8, 440) plays A4; noTone(8) stops it. Only one tone at a time per board.
Typical audible range: 200 Hz to 5 kHz; piezos are loudest around 2–4 kHz.
pitfalls: Using delay() inside a melody blocks everything else — use millis() for lights that keep blinking.

learn.summary: A hobby servo turns to an angle you command with a pulse train: a 1–2 ms pulse every 20 ms maps to 0–180°. The Servo library generates the pulses; the servo needs 5 V power and a shared ground.
pinout: signal (orange/yellow): to a digital pin, e.g. D9.
vcc (red): 5V / VIN — at least 4.5 V.
gnd (brown/black): GND.
tips: servo.attach(9); servo.write(90); — 90° is the middle position.
Power the servo from 5V/VIN, never from a GPIO pin: it can draw hundreds of mA while moving.
On the ESP32 the 3.3 V signal is fine; use ESP32Servo.h and power from VIN.
pitfalls: A servo powered from 3V3 stutters or does nothing — it is unpowered below 4.5 V here.
Forgetting the shared GND leaves the signal without a reference.

learn.summary: A 16x2 character LCD with an I2C backpack shows two lines of 16 characters using just two data wires (SDA, SCL) plus power. The LiquidCrystal_I2C library talks to it at address 0x27.
pinout: gnd: GND.
vcc: 5V (the backlight and logic want 5 V).
sda: A4 (Uno/Nano) or GPIO21 (ESP32).
scl: A5 (Uno/Nano) or GPIO22 (ESP32).
tips: LiquidCrystal_I2C lcd(0x27, 16, 2); lcd.init(); lcd.backlight(); lcd.print("Hello");
lcd.setCursor(column, row) before printing the second line: lcd.setCursor(0, 1).
Some backpacks use address 0x3F — change the addr prop and the constructor to match.
formulas: Two wires, up to 127 devices — each needs a different address
pitfalls: Wrong address or swapped SDA/SCL: the screen lights but shows nothing.
Powered from 3V3 the backlight is dim and text may vanish (needs ≥ 4.5 V).

learn.summary: A 0.96" SSD1306 OLED is a 128×64 pixel monochrome display driven over I2C. Draw text and shapes with Adafruit_GFX, then call display() to push the frame.
pinout: vcc: 3V3 or 5V (the module regulates; needs ≥ 3 V).
gnd: GND.
scl: I2C clock (A5 / GPIO22).
sda: I2C data (A4 / GPIO21).
tips: Adafruit_SSD1306 display(128, 64, &Wire); display.begin(SSD1306_SWITCHCAPVCC, 0x3C);
Nothing appears until display.display() — and clearDisplay() first when redrawing.
Pixels are OLEDs: white pixels use power, black ones are off.
pitfalls: begin() returns false when the address does not match or SDA/SCL are swapped.
Mind the pin order: many modules are VCC-GND-SCL-SDA, others GND-VCC.

learn.summary: A seven-segment display is eight LEDs (segments a–g plus the decimal point) sharing a common cathode. Light the right combination to show a digit: 0 = a b c d e f, 1 = b c, and so on.
pinout: Top row: g, f, com, a, b.  Bottom row: e, d, com, c, dp.
Both com pins are the same common cathode — connect either one to GND.
Segments are laid out a (top), b (top right), c (bottom right), d (bottom), e (bottom left), f (top left), g (middle).
tips: Give every segment its own 220 Ω resistor; a single resistor on com makes digits dimmer the more segments are lit.
Store the digit patterns in a byte array and loop over the 7 segment pins.
formulas: Per segment: I = (Vsrc − 1.8 V) / (R + Rpin + 10 Ω)
Eight segments × 12 mA ≈ 100 mA total from the supply
pitfalls: Eight pins at once can exceed the total current an Uno should source at the same time — use higher resistors or fewer segments.

learn.summary: A NeoPixel (WS2812B) ring is a chain of addressable RGB LEDs. One data wire carries colours for every pixel; the library handles the timing. Each pixel can draw up to 60 mA at full white.
pinout: din: data in — to a digital pin (through a 330–470 Ω resistor in real builds).
vcc: 5V / VIN (≥ 4.5 V).
gnd: GND.
tips: Adafruit_NeoPixel ring(12, PIN, NEO_GRB + NEO_KHZ800); ring.begin(); ring.setPixelColor(0, ring.Color(255, 0, 0)); ring.show();
Set ring.setBrightness(40) — full brightness on 12 pixels is blinding and hungry.
A 3.3 V ESP32 data signal works in the simulator and usually in real life; a level shifter makes it reliable.
formulas: Max current ≈ pixels × 60 mA  (12 pixels → 720 mA at full white)
pitfalls: Powering 12 pixels from the 500 mA USB budget at full white overloads it — dim them.
Data goes into DIN, not DOUT; the arrow on the ring shows the direction.

learn.summary: A small DC motor spins when current flows through it; reverse the current and it spins the other way. It draws far more than a pin can supply, so drive it through a transistor.
pinout: p1 / p2: the two motor leads — no polarity, just direction.
tips: Wire: 5V → motor → collector of an NPN, emitter → GND, base ← pin through 1 kΩ.
Add a flyback diode across the motor (cathode to +) to absorb the voltage spike when it stops.
Speed follows current — PWM on the transistor base gives smooth speed control.
formulas: Stall current ≈ 5 V / 20 Ω = 250 mA (way over the 40 mA pin limit)
pitfalls: Connecting the motor straight to a pin overloads the pin and stalls the sketch's LEDs too.

learn.summary: A tactile pushbutton connects its two sides only while pressed. The legs come in two pairs that are always joined internally, so straddle the breadboard so that each pair sits in a different row.
pinout: a1 / a2: one side (always connected to each other).
b1 / b2: the other side, two rows over.
Pressed: a ↔ b closes with about 0.1 Ω.
tips: Wire one side to GND and the other to a pin set to INPUT_PULLUP: reads HIGH released, LOW pressed.
Without a pull-up or pull-down the released pin floats and flickers randomly.
For a pull-down version: 10 kΩ from pin to GND, other side of the button to 5V — reads HIGH when pressed.
formulas: Pull-up: released V = Vcc (through ~35 kΩ), pressed V ≈ 0 V
pitfalls: Rotated so both pairs sit in the same strip, the button is permanently "pressed".
digitalRead on a floating pin gives random values — always add a pull.

learn.summary: A potentiometer is a resistor with a sliding contact (wiper). Between the ends it is always 10 kΩ; between an end and the wiper the resistance follows the knob. Wired end-to-end across the supply it becomes an adjustable voltage divider.
pinout: end1: to 5V (or 3V3 on the ESP32).
wiper: the middle pin — to an analog input.
end2: to GND.
tips: analogRead(A0) then gives 0 at one end and 1023 (4095 on ESP32) at the other.
map(value, 0, 1023, 0, 255) turns a knob position into a PWM level.
Swap end1 and end2 to reverse the direction of the knob.
formulas: Rend1–wiper = R × (1 − position), Rwiper–end2 = R × position
pitfalls: On the ESP32 feed end1 from 3V3, not VIN — 5 V on the wiper burns the GPIO.
Wiring the wiper to a supply forces current through a tiny resistance at the knob's end.

learn.summary: A light-dependent resistor (photoresistor) has high resistance in the dark (~200 kΩ) and low in bright light (~1 kΩ). Pair it with a fixed 10 kΩ resistor to turn light into a voltage an analog pin can read.
pinout: p1 / p2: no polarity.
Spans 3 holes.
tips: Divider: 5V → LDR → A0 → 10 kΩ → GND. Brighter light → lower LDR resistance → higher voltage at A0.
Pick the fixed resistor near the LDR's mid-range (10 kΩ) for the most sensitive readings.
Use the light slider on the part to test day/night thresholds without waiting for sunset.
pitfalls: LDR straight into an input with no fixed resistor: the pin floats at Vcc regardless of light.

learn.summary: A touch pad is just a piece of metal or copper tape wired to an ESP32 touch pin. touchRead() measures the pad's capacitance: it drops from about 70 to around 15 when a finger is on it.
pinout: pad: wire to a touch-capable GPIO (T0 = GPIO4, T2 = GPIO2 …).
tips: if (touchRead(T0) < 40) — a threshold halfway between idle (~70) and touched (~15).
Only ESP32 boards have touch hardware; on an Uno the pad does nothing.
pitfalls: Long wires and nearby metal raise the idle reading — calibrate at startup instead of hard-coding.

learn.summary: A PIR motion sensor watches for moving body heat and raises its OUT pin to 3.3 V while motion is detected. It has its own regulator, so it wants 5 V power but is safe for 3.3 V inputs.
pinout: vcc: 5V / VIN (≥ 4.5 V).
out: 3.3 V HIGH on motion — to any digital input.
gnd: GND.
tips: pinMode(pin, INPUT); if (digitalRead(pin) == HIGH) — no pull-up needed.
Real sensors hold OUT high for a few seconds after motion; toggle the "motion" switch here to test.
formulas: OUT = 3.3 V when motion, 0 V otherwise (through ~50 Ω)
pitfalls: Powered from 3V3 the module is unpowered and OUT stays low forever.

learn.summary: The DHT22 measures temperature (−40…80 °C) and humidity (0…100 %) and reports them over a single data wire using its own timing protocol. The DHT library does the decoding.
pinout: vcc: 3V3 or 5V (≥ 3 V).
data: to any digital pin (a 10 kΩ pull-up to VCC is built into most modules).
gnd: GND.
tips: DHT dht(PIN, DHT22); dht.begin(); float t = dht.readTemperature(); float h = dht.readHumidity();
Readings take up to 2 s each — do not poll faster than every 2000 ms.
Drag the temperature/humidity sliders to simulate a warm, humid afternoon.
formulas: Heat index and dew point are computed by the library from t and h
Data line idles HIGH at VCC; unpowered → readings are NaN
pitfalls: isnan(t) is how you detect a missing sensor — check it before printing.

learn.summary: The BME280 is a precise environmental sensor: temperature, barometric pressure and humidity over I2C. Pressure lets you estimate altitude and spot weather changes.
pinout: vin: 3V3 or 5V (≥ 3 V; the module regulates).
gnd: GND.
scl: I2C clock (A5 / GPIO22).
sda: I2C data (A4 / GPIO21).
tips: Adafruit_BME280 bme; if (!bme.begin(0x76)) Serial.println("no sensor");
bme.readTemperature(), bme.readPressure() / 100.0F (hPa), bme.readHumidity().
Publish readings over MQTT every few seconds for a weather station.
pitfalls: begin() returns false with the wrong address or swapped SDA/SCL.

learn.summary: The HC-SR04 measures distance with sound: pulse TRIG for 10 µs, and ECHO goes HIGH for as long as the ping takes to bounce back. It runs on 5 V, so its 5 V ECHO must be divided down for an ESP32.
pinout: vcc: 5V / VIN (≥ 4.5 V).
trig: any digital output.
echo: 5 V pulse output — safe for an Uno, needs a divider or level shifter for an ESP32.
gnd: GND.
tips: digitalWrite(TRIG, HIGH); delayMicroseconds(10); digitalWrite(TRIG, LOW); long us = pulseIn(ECHO, HIGH);
Distance in cm = us / 58.3 (sound travels there and back at 343 m/s).
ESP32: ECHO → 1 kΩ → GPIO, GPIO → 2.2 kΩ → GND gives 5 V × 2.2 / 3.2 = 3.44 V.
pitfalls: ECHO straight into an ESP32 GPIO burns the pin (5 V > 3.6 V).
A 10 kΩ / 1 kΩ divider is the wrong way round: 0.45 V never reads HIGH.

learn.summary: A 5 V relay module is an electrically controlled switch: a small signal on IN energises a coil that flips a mechanical contact between COM–NC (normally closed) and COM–NO (normally open).
pinout: vcc: 5V / VIN.
gnd: GND.
in: control signal from a pin (HIGH = on).
com: common contact.
no: normally open — connected to com only when on.
nc: normally closed — connected to com only when off.

A 3.3 V ESP32 signal only just reaches the 0.6 × 5 V = 3 V threshold — power the module from 3V3-compatible relays or use a transistor in real builds.

learn.summary: A bidirectional logic level shifter translates signals between a 5 V side (HV) and a 3.3 V side (LV). Each channel has a pull-up to its own supply; pulling one side LOW pulls the other side LOW too, so a 5 V HIGH becomes a clean 3.3 V HIGH.
pinout: hv: 5 V reference (5V / VIN).  lv: 3.3 V reference (3V3).  gnd_h / gnd_l: GND (both).
hv1–hv4: 5 V side of channels 1–4.  lv1–lv4: 3.3 V side of the same channels.
tips: Feed HV from VIN and LV from 3V3 on the ESP32 — both references are required for it to work.
Sensor outputs (HC-SR04 echo) go into HVn; read LVn on the GPIO. MCU outputs go into LVn to drive 5 V inputs on HVn.
Idle channels sit HIGH on both sides thanks to the 10 kΩ pull-ups.
formulas: V(LVn) = V(lv) when idle or HIGH; ≈ 0 V when either side is pulled LOW
pitfalls: Unpowered (hv or lv below 1 V): channels are open and nothing passes.
It shifts logic, not power — do not draw motor current through it.
